items.original_title: FinancialJuice: Crédit Agricole: Midterm Outcome Adds to USD Downside Risks

evidence.headline: FinancialJuice: Crédit Agricole: Midterm Outcome Adds to USD Downside Risks
evidence.snippet: The midterm result has increased concerns that tighter regulation could slow AI investment, forcing investors to reassess US tech and the dollar. A weaker AI boom would be negative for the US growth story, while heavy reliance on foreign buying of US technology stocks to finance the current-account deficit may also reduce the dollar’s safe-haven appeal when risk aversion is driven by AI-related market stress. Historically, the dollar has fallen by around 3% in the months after midterms that produced Democratic control of Congress under a Republican president. Legislative gridlock and the risk of future government shutdowns could add further pressure, with the next funding deadline on 11 December. Gold and the CHF are seen as the clearest hedges against a politically driven USD selloff, while unresolved Middle East tensions remain another near-term risk. Attention next week turns to US CPI and PPI, UK GDP and central-bank commentary.

items.original_title: FinancialJuice: Bank of America: Record Oil Supply Shock Leaves Market More Vulnerable to Further Disruption

evidence.headline: FinancialJuice: Bank of America: Record Oil Supply Shock Leaves Market More Vulnerable to Further Disruption
evidence.snippet: Global oil supply disruptions have reached unprecedented levels in 2026, exceeding anything in the historical data since 1965. Large inventories built during earlier periods of surplus helped absorb the initial shock, but those buffers are now being depleted, with particularly heavy draws in China and declining strategic stocks across OECD economies. Refinery outages in the Middle East and Russia have further tightened product markets, leaving the system with much less protection against another major disruption. Despite the physical tightness, global economic activity has held up better than expected. Brent spreads, freight costs and refining margins all point to scarcity, but longer-dated oil prices remain much lower, implying expectations that supply eventually normalises. Demand has also remained resilient, supported by strong US growth, AI investment and the US position as a major net energy exporter. The shock has so far been absorbed through inventories, conservation and rerouting rather than large-scale demand destruction. Brent forecasts remain at $96 for H2 2026 and $80 for 2027, but the range of outcomes is wide. A ceasefire across the US-Iran, Saudi-Houthi or Russia-Ukraine conflicts could restore supply and push oil toward $80 or lower next year. A prolonged “neither war nor peace” environment could keep Brent around triple digits, while renewed major US-Iran conflict could push prices toward $150 a barrel in 2027 given lower inventories, limited shale responsiveness and weak short-run demand elasticity.
